## Overview

::: {.summary}

📘 **forms**
An HTML form **collects user input**: a login, a search box, a signup, a shopping cart. The `<form>` element wraps **input controls** (text fields, checkboxes, radio buttons, drop-downs, buttons) and, when it is submitted, sends their values to a server.

In React, forms are where **state and events** meet: every keystroke is an event and every field value becomes state. So first we need to know the plain HTML form very well.

:::

---

## The `<form>` element

``` {.html .code-overflow-wrap filename="form.html"}
<form action="/register" method="post">
  <!-- form controls go here -->
</form>
```

- `action`: the URL where the data is sent when the form is submitted. If it is missing, the form is sent to the current page.
- `method`: how the data is sent:
  - `get` (default): data goes in the URL (`/search?q=react`). Good for searches, **never for passwords**.
  - `post`: data goes in the body of the HTTP request. Use it for anything private or that changes data.
- When the form is submitted, the browser builds a list of `name=value` pairs, one for each control **that has a `name`**.

::: {.callout-important}
## No `name`, no data
A control without a `name` attribute is **not sent** with the form. In plain HTML `name` is the key of each value; in React we'll often use it to know which field changed.
:::

## A complete form

``` {.html .code-overflow-wrap filename="signup.html"}
<form action="/register" method="post">
  <label for="name">Name</label>
  <input type="text" id="name" name="name" placeholder="Your name" required>

  <label for="email">Email</label>
  <input type="email" id="email" name="email" required>

  <label for="pwd">Password</label>
  <input type="password" id="pwd" name="pwd" minlength="8" required>

  <label for="age">Age</label>
  <input type="number" id="age" name="age" min="16" max="99">

  <fieldset>
    <legend>Level</legend>
    <label><input type="radio" name="level" value="junior" checked> Junior</label>
    <label><input type="radio" name="level" value="senior"> Senior</label>
  </fieldset>

  <label><input type="checkbox" name="news" value="yes"> Send me news</label>

  <label for="course">Course</label>
  <select id="course" name="course">
    <option value="">-- choose one --</option>
    <option value="react">React</option>
    <option value="spring">Spring Boot</option>
  </select>

  <label for="msg">Message</label>
  <textarea id="msg" name="msg" rows="4" cols="40"></textarea>

  <button type="submit">Send</button>
  <button type="reset">Clear</button>
</form>
```

## Form elements

### `<label>`

`<label>` gives a **visible name** to a control. Link it with `for` = the `id` of the input, or wrap the input inside the label:

``` html
<label for="email">Email</label>
<input type="email" id="email" name="email">

<label><input type="checkbox" name="terms"> I accept the terms</label>
```

Clicking the label focuses (or toggles) the control: a bigger click target, which really helps on mobile and for small checkboxes and radio buttons.

### `<input>` and its types

`<input>` is the most important form element, and it is **empty** (no end tag). What it shows depends on its `type`:

| `type`      | What it shows                                         |
|-------------|-------------------------------------------------------|
| `text`      | One-line text field (the default)                     |
| `email`     | Text field that must contain an email address         |
| `password`  | Text field with hidden characters                     |
| `number`    | Numeric field with up/down arrows                     |
| `date`, `time` | A date or time picker                              |
| `checkbox`  | On/off box; many can be selected                      |
| `radio`     | Option button; only one per `name` group can be selected |
| `range`     | A slider between `min` and `max`                      |
| `color`     | A colour picker                                       |
| `file`      | A button to choose a file to upload                   |
| `search`, `tel`, `url` | Text fields with special keyboards on mobile |
| `hidden`    | Not shown, but its value is sent                      |
| `submit`, `reset`, `button` | Buttons (prefer `<button>`)           |

: Most used input types {.striped .hover}

::: {.column-margin}
On a phone, `type="email"`, `type="tel"` or `type="number"` opens the right keyboard. Choosing the correct type is free usability.
:::

### `<select>` and `<option>`

A drop-down list. The `value` of the selected `<option>` is what gets sent. Add `selected` to preselect one, or `multiple` on `<select>` to allow several.

### `<textarea>`

A multi-line text field. Its size is set with `rows` and `cols` (or with CSS). Unlike `<input>`, in HTML its initial text goes **between the tags**.

### `<button>`

| `type`     | What it does                                   |
|------------|------------------------------------------------|
| `submit`   | Submits the form (the **default** inside a form) |
| `reset`    | Resets all controls to their initial values    |
| `button`   | Does nothing by itself: you add a click handler |

::: {.callout-warning}
## The default type is `submit`
A `<button>` inside a `<form>` with no `type` is a submit button. A "Show password" or "Add item" button will suddenly submit (and reload) the page. Always write `type="button"` for buttons that should not submit.
:::

### `<fieldset>` and `<legend>`

`<fieldset>` groups related controls (like a group of radio buttons) and `<legend>` gives the group a caption.

## Input attributes

| Attribute     | What it does                                                   |
|---------------|----------------------------------------------------------------|
| `name`        | Key of the value when the form is sent                         |
| `value`       | Initial value (or the value sent for checkboxes/radios)        |
| `placeholder` | Hint text shown while the field is empty (not a label!)        |
| `required`    | The field must be filled in before submitting                  |
| `min` / `max` | Minimum / maximum for `number`, `range`, `date`                |
| `minlength` / `maxlength` | Minimum / maximum number of characters             |
| `pattern`     | A regular expression the value must match                      |
| `step`        | Allowed step for numbers (`step="0.01"` for prices)            |
| `checked`     | Preselects a checkbox or radio                                 |
| `disabled`    | Field can't be used **and is not sent**                        |
| `readonly`    | Field can't be edited, but it is sent                          |
| `autofocus`   | Gets the focus when the page loads                             |
| `autocomplete`| Lets the browser autofill (`email`, `name`, `off`...)          |

: Most used input attributes {.striped .hover}

## Built-in validation

The browser can **validate a form for free** before sending it: if a rule fails, it shows a message and does not submit.

``` {.html .code-overflow-wrap filename="validation.html"}
<form>
  <!-- must not be empty -->
  <input type="text" name="user" required>

  <!-- must look like an email -->
  <input type="email" name="email" required>

  <!-- between 1 and 10 -->
  <input type="number" name="qty" min="1" max="10">

  <!-- a Spanish postcode: exactly 5 digits -->
  <input type="text" name="cp" pattern="[0-9]{5}" title="5 digits, e.g. 08001">

  <button type="submit">Send</button>
</form>
```

- The `title` text is shown in the error message when `pattern` fails.
- CSS can style the state with the `:valid` and `:invalid` pseudo-classes.
- JavaScript can check it too: `input.checkValidity()` and `input.validity`.
- `novalidate` on `<form>` turns browser validation off (useful when you write your own in React).

::: {.callout-important}
## Validate on the server too
Client validation is for **user experience**. Anyone can skip it (dev tools, Postman, curl), so the backend (Spring Boot, for example) must validate again.
:::

## Accessibility basics

- **Every control needs a label.** A `placeholder` disappears when you type, so it is not a label.
- Link label and input with `for`/`id` (or wrap the input).
- Group radio buttons and checkboxes with `<fieldset>` and `<legend>`.
- Use the **right element**: `<button>` for actions, `<a>` for navigation, never a clickable `<div>`.
- Use the correct `type` and `autocomplete` so browsers, password managers and screen readers understand the field.
- Keep the **keyboard** working: Tab moves between fields, Enter submits, Space toggles checkboxes. Native elements give you this for free.

## Forms in React

In React the same elements are used, with two changes:

1. The form is usually handled in JavaScript: we listen to `onSubmit` and call `event.preventDefault()` so the page does not reload (see [Events and the DOM](/reactjs/reactjs-what-html-events.qmd)).
2. Each field is often a **controlled input**: its `value` comes from state and `onChange` updates that state.

``` {.jsx .code-overflow-wrap filename="NameField.jsx"}
const [name, setName] = useState("");

<input
  type="text"
  name="name"
  value={name}
  onChange={(e) => setName(e.target.value)}
  required
/>
```

The full example is in [From HTML to JSX](/reactjs/reactjs-what-html-jsx.qmd). See also [React JS: useState](/reactjs/reactjs-hook-state.qmd) and [React JS App: events](/reactjs/reactjs-app-events.qmd).
